prompt: The article mentions several indicators. List those related to a goal and those related to a main line of action. You can indicate the arguments or hypotheses justifying your answer. (5 points)
modelAnswer: The two goals are debt reduction (leverage below 3× EBITDA) and growth faster than the market. Indicators related to a goal: net debt / EBITDA (4.1×, target < 3×), revenue growth (+9%), RevPAR growth (+6%, accepted as a growth indicator; can also be argued as a lever since it combines price and occupancy); the EBITDA margin rate is presented by the CFO as the goal indicator for debt reduction (see Q2). Indicators related to lines of action: occupancy rate (78%), share of direct bookings (38% – lever to cut commissions and improve margin), guest satisfaction (8.7/10 – not presented as a goal), energy consumption per room night (−12% – cost lever). 1 point per correctly classified and justified indicator, max. 5.
keyPoints: Goals: debt reduction and growth
Goal indicators: net debt/EBITDA, revenue (and RevPAR) growth
Line-of-action indicators: occupancy rate, share of direct bookings
Line-of-action indicators: guest satisfaction, energy per room night
Justification can rescue a debatable classification (RevPAR, EBITDA margin)

basis.ref: im Stil des Mock up exam, Part 1 – Q1

topic: Relevance of the EBITDA margin for debt reduction
prompt: Does the EBITDA margin rate seem to you to be well chosen to steer the debt-reduction objective as expressed in the article? Justify your answer. (4 points)
modelAnswer: Only partially – rather no. EBITDA can be used as a proxy of operating cash flow, and leverage is expressed as net debt / EBITDA, so the choice is not absurd. But (1) a margin rate measures profitability relative to sales, not the cash actually available to repay debt; (2) debt is repaid with free cash flow, i.e. after capital expenditure (the €40m renovation programme!), working capital, taxes and interest, which EBITDA ignores; (3) the objective is itself expressed as a ratio (net debt / EBITDA < 3), which should be the goal indicator. Better: net debt / EBITDA and free cash flow (or change in net debt). 2 points for the inconsistency, 2 points for the right indicators.
keyPoints: EBITDA is a cash proxy – but a margin rate measures profitability
Debt is repaid from free cash flow (after capex, WC, taxes, interest)
€40m renovation capex ignored by EBITDA
Use net debt/EBITDA and free cash flow

prompt: What can you say about the "objectives" as they appear in the framework? Comment precisely on 4 different points (positive or negative). (8 points)
modelAnswer: Possible points (2 points each): (1) Positive: O2 is specific, measurable, targeted (18%) and time-bound (20n+1) and translates the managing director's main goal. (2) O4 is not an objective but a line of action (how to get there), and it contradicts both the medium-range positioning with little room on prices and O2 (lower prices reduce the margin). (3) O1 is vague: no target, no horizon, and growth in revenue is not a goal in itself for the MD – it is only a means if it is profitable; it overlaps with O3. (4) O3 is targeted but has no time horizon and is the only market-share target: the agreed targets for Bermuda shorts (25%) and sweatsuits (20%) appear as a CPV (CPV 5) instead of an objective. (5) The hierarchy is unclear: the main goal (margin) should be at the top, the others subordinated to it.

O4 is a line of action and contradicts positioning/margin

prompt: What can you say about the framework as a whole? Comment precisely on 3 different points (positive or negative). (6 points)
modelAnswer: Possible points (2 points each): (1) 4 objectives and 10 CPVs = 14 dimensions: a manageable size for a steering dashboard (+). (2) The main goal (O2, margin) is supported only by production/purchasing levers, while the sales levers point at volume (O1, O3); no CPV deals with price discipline or the contribution margin, although price is the risk in a medium-range positioning. (3) Crosses hide negative effects: the 2.2% bonus and the two hires increase selling costs (− on O2), outsourcing has a cost (− or ? on O2) – "+" and "−" would show the trade-offs. (4) Some causal links are questionable: outsourcing parka assembly is mainly a capacity lever for growth (O1/O3), not only a margin lever; subcontractor lead times (CPV 9) matter for all sales, not just market share. (5) Most CPVs are linked to one or two objectives only; few are truly transversal.
keyPoints: 14 dimensions: manageable (+)
Margin goal supported only by production levers; no price/contribution lever
Use + / −: bonus and hires cost money, outsourcing trade-off
Questionable causal links (CPV 3, CPV 9)
Few transversal CPVs

prompt: What is the most relevant type of responsibility centre to qualify the roasting plant? 1) Cost centre 2) Revenue centre 3) Profit centre 4) Investment centre. Explain your answer (2 lines max). (3 points)
modelAnswer: Answer 1 – cost centre. The plant controls its production costs (staff, energy, maintenance, green coffee consumption per bag) but not revenues (it roasts to order for the agencies), not its investments and not the purchase price of green coffee (central purchasing). It holds no finished stock. Its cost indicator should therefore exclude the price of green coffee (controllability principle).
keyPoints: Cost centre
Controls production costs and consumption, not revenues
No investments, no finished stock
Green coffee price not controllable → exclude price effects

basis.ref: im Stil des Mock up exam, Part 3 – Q1

prompt: What is the most relevant type of responsibility centre to qualify the regional agencies? 1) Cost centre 2) Revenue centre 3) Profit centre 4) Investment centre. Explain your answer (2 lines max). (2 points)
modelAnswer: Answer 3 – profit centre. Agencies act on revenues (volumes, discounts) and on their direct costs (staff, vans, premises), but not on investments, which are decided at headquarters. Nuances: they do not control production costs (their indicator should be a contribution after their own costs), but they do control short-term assets (stocks, receivables through payment terms) – a charge on working capital should be considered.
keyPoints: Profit centre
Control revenues (discounts) and direct costs
No investments; production cost unknown/uncontrolled
Nuance: they manage stocks and receivables → charge on working capital
